rationale: Start with a broad gradient ending at high organic to observe all 10 compounds with low truncation risk. This establishes the elution window and critical pairs before refining gradient slope and temperature.

Raise temperature by 5 C while holding the gradient fixed to test selectivity around the sole unresolved pair. All peaks currently elute comfortably within 10 minutes, so improving that pair could reach the maximum CRF without slowing the gradient.

The critical pair nearly co-eluted at 45 C, so test 35 C to move its selectivity in the opposite direction. Keep the gradient unchanged to isolate temperature effects and check whether neighboring pairs remain resolved.

Test beyond the apparent selectivity crossover near 45 C, where the co-eluting pair may separate again in reversed order. Keeping the gradient fixed reveals whether this higher-temperature region resolves that pair without creating another critical overlap.
Make the gradient modestly shallower at the best temperature to improve the remaining R = 1.29 pair. The last peak at 7.25 minutes leaves room to gain resolution without incurring a time penalty.

Injection 5 achieves the maximum CRF and remains the benchmark. Test a lower starting organic fraction with a shorter gradient to alter selectivity around the critical pairs and seek full resolution with earlier final elution.

Shorten the fastest fully resolved method by one gradient-time step to test its speed limit. Both critical pairs have little resolution margin, so retain injection 6 as the benchmark if the steeper gradient pushes either below 1.5.

Test the upper temperature limit with the faster gradient to determine whether selectivity changes can restore full resolution, including possible elution-order reversals. Injection 6 remains the fastest confirmed method with CRF 1.000.

The high-temperature route loses resolution when shortened, so explore the low-temperature selectivity regime with the same fast gradient. This tests whether further elution-order changes can separate the central cluster while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes.

Test a higher starting organic fraction and shorter gradient at 40 C to explore a different selectivity route to faster separation. The maximum score is already secured; injection 6 remains the fastest fully resolved benchmark.

Raise the starting organic fraction one step from injection 5 to shorten elution while retaining its shallower gradient. Its two tightest pairs had R = 1.77 and 1.57, so this tests whether that resolution margin supports a faster fully resolved method.

Test a faster gradient at 60 C with higher starting organic to move the troublesome central pair beyond its apparent selectivity crossover. This explores a potentially faster, reversed-order separation while retaining injection 6 as the fully resolved benchmark.

Raise starting organic one step to test whether the remaining central overlap separates further in the reversed-order regime. Check the first pair and neighboring central pair carefully, since both may lose resolution as retention decreases.

Test whether a steeper gradient further separates the reversed central pair at 60 C, while lowering starting organic to protect the first pair. This explores a faster separation regime without displacing injection 6 as the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Return to 40 C with lower starting organic to test whether the central cluster can be resolved on a faster gradient in this temperature regime. The 60 C experiments introduced competing overlaps, so retain injection 6 as the fastest fully resolved benchmark.

Use an intermediate gradient slope between injections 4 and 5 to target full resolution with less retention than injection 5. Lowering the endpoint to 0.90 makes this fine adjustment while retaining ample elution strength.

Fine-tune the gradient slope just below injection 16’s to lift its R = 1.47 pair above 1.5 while preserving the neighboring pair’s margin. This should provide a shorter programmed gradient than the confirmed maximum-score methods, with final elution still comfortably below 10 minutes.

Test the intermediate-temperature selectivity regime using the fast gradient from injection 12. Cooling may separate its overlapping central pair, but the full central cluster must be checked for new overlaps; injection 6 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-score method.

Test a shallower gradient at 60 C to recover separation of the pair that nearly co-eluted in injection 8. This may offer a maximum-score alternative with more margin in the neighboring pair, while the last peak is expected to remain below 10 minutes.

Test a slope between the fully resolved injection 6 and the faster but unresolved injection 7. This narrows the speed–resolution boundary at the best temperature while retaining injection 6 as the fastest confirmed maximum-score method.

Refine around the confirmed maximum-score methods with a slope between injections 5 and 17. This targets slightly more margin for the tightest pair than injection 17 while keeping final elution below 10 minutes.

Make injection 11’s gradient shallower to restore its unresolved pair while exploiting its larger margin in the neighboring pair. This tests a potentially more robust maximum-score method; injection 6 remains the fastest fully resolved option.

Lower the endpoint one step from injection 22 to bring its R = 1.41 pair above 1.5, with final elution expected near 9 minutes. This targets a maximum-score alternative with greater resolution margin; injection 6 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

With maximum CRF already secured, test one shallower step from injection 23 for a larger minimum-resolution margin while targeting final elution below 10 minutes. Injection 6 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Shorten injection 24’s gradient and slightly increase its slope to reduce final retention while targeting full resolution with useful margin. Injection 6 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-score method, with all peaks resolved by 7.60 minutes.
